paras: The Mahanoy City threatened lynching of 1881 was an incident in early July 1881 in which a crowd in Mahanoy City, Pennsylvania, went after a man accused of a remark approving of the attempt on President Garfield's life. One account said the crowd had a rope around his neck before letting him go, while another said he denied the remark and was left unharmed.

A Tamaqua correspondent of the Daily Republican wrote on July 5 that the attempted assassination of the President had "created intense feeling here." The letter, headed as a report from the mountains of Schuylkill County, placed Mahanoy City "near" Tamaqua.

According to the correspondent, "a man named Refowitch" in Mahanoy City "came near near being lynched" for "some disloyal remark." The letter said "they had the rope around his neck" when he begged so hard that they let him off.

A short item in two other Pennsylvania papers described an unnamed shopkeeper in Mahanoy City "reported to have made some remarks approving of the assassination of President Garfield." In that version, "a large deputation of excited citizens" came to him intending to administer "summary punishment," but he denied the remark and, persuaded by a number of citizens, the crowd did not molest him. No article gives the man's race.
No report of an arrest or of any official action against the crowd appears in the coverage.

The Daily Republican mentioned the incident on July 8 in a single paragraph of a long letter about summering in the Schuylkill mountains, between notes on the Fourth of July and a militia inspection. The New Bloomfield Times on July 12 and the Juniata Sentinel and Republican on July 13 carried the shopkeeper item word for word, the latter in its "State Items" column, without headline or comment. None of the reports criticized the crowd; the correspondent offered the episode as a measure of local feeling about the President.

The accounts differ on what the crowd did: the Daily Republican's correspondent described a rope around the man's neck, while the shared item said he "was not molested." They also differ on the date, which the shared item gives as "Saturday" in the New Bloomfield Times and "the 4th of July" in the Juniata Sentinel. Neither version comes from a local Mahanoy City source, and no article states that Refowitch and the shopkeeper were the same man.

reader.title: Mahanoy City threatened lynching of 1881
bases: A1 describes a crowd that put a rope around a man's neck and nearly lynched him, while A2 and A3 describe a crowd that came to administer 'summary punishment' but left him unharmed; the episode is at most an attempted or threatened lynching, and no report gives anyone's race.

No one was killed: A1 says the man was let off after begging and A2/A3 say he 'was not molested'; a crowd (A2/A3 'a large deputation of excited citizens') acted without lawful authority to punish a remark, so it was at most an attempted or threatened lynching.

A1 (a correspondent's secondhand letter) says a rope was placed around the man's neck, while the item printed in A2 and A3 says he denied the remark and was not molested; the two reports agree only that a crowd in Mahanoy City confronted a man over a remark about the attack on the President.

accounts.label: Tamaqua correspondent
accounts.gist: In Mahanoy City a man named Refowitch came near being lynched for a disloyal remark; the crowd had a rope around his neck but let him off when he begged.

accounts.label: State news item
accounts.gist: A large deputation of excited citizens went to punish a shopkeeper said to have approved of the assassination; he denied it, other citizens intervened, and he was not molested.

framing.detail: A1 mentions the incident in one paragraph of a travel letter as evidence that the attempt on the President 'created intense feeling here', without comment on the crowd.
A2 and A3 print the same short item, without headline or comment, among other Pennsylvania news.

versions.value: Rope put around his neck; let off when he begged
He denied the remark and was not molested

conflicts.note: A1 is a secondhand line in a correspondent's letter; A2/A3 are one shared item. Neither is clearly local or sworn, and no article says these are the same incident; the link rests on place and subject.
The same item gives two different days; A1's letter, dated July 5, gives no day.
